# Multi-Area OSPF Troubleshooting Lab (v2)

You're the network engineer for a small enterprise WAN running live in GNS3: an edge router with two ISP uplinks, two hub routers, four branch routers, and ten hosts. The network has drifted from its design and users are reporting connectivity problems, but nobody has pinned down what is failing or why. There may be more than one fault, anywhere in the lab. Your job is to find every fault, fix each one at its root, and show that the network matches its design again.

This run is unattended, so nobody will be around to answer questions. When you hit a judgment call, make the call a careful engineer would make and explain it in your report.

## Access

Every device has an out-of-band management interface on 192.168.122.0/24 that you can reach over SSH from this machine. Python 3 and netmiko are available. With 19 devices, a small reusable script is the practical way to run commands across them.

| Device | Platform | Mgmt address | Mgmt interface | netmiko `device_type` | Login |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| HQ-Edge | VyOS | 192.168.122.11 | eth3 | `vyos` | vyos / test |
| Hub-A | VyOS | 192.168.122.12 | eth4 | `vyos` | vyos / test |
| Hub-B | VyOS | 192.168.122.13 | eth3 | `vyos` | vyos / test |
| ISP-A | VyOS | 192.168.122.14 | eth3 | `vyos` | vyos / test |
| ISP-B | VyOS | 192.168.122.15 | eth3 | `vyos` | vyos / test |
| Branch-1 | MikroTik RouterOS 7 | 192.168.122.21 | ether4 | `mikrotik_routeros` | admin / test |
| Branch-2 | MikroTik RouterOS 7 | 192.168.122.22 | ether4 | `mikrotik_routeros` | admin / test |
| Branch-3 | MikroTik RouterOS 7 | 192.168.122.23 | ether4 | `mikrotik_routeros` | admin / test |
| Branch-4 | MikroTik RouterOS 7 | 192.168.122.24 | ether4 | `mikrotik_routeros` | admin / test |
| B1-PC1, B1-PC2 | Alpine Linux | 192.168.122.31, .32 | eth3 | `linux` | root / alpine |
| B2-PC1, B2-PC2 | Alpine Linux | 192.168.122.33, .34 | eth3 | `linux` | root / alpine |
| B3-PC1, B3-PC2 | Alpine Linux | 192.168.122.35, .36 | eth3 | `linux` | root / alpine |
| B4-PC1 … B4-PC4 | Alpine Linux | 192.168.122.37 … .40 | eth3 | `linux` | root / alpine |

Hub-A is the exception: its management interface is eth4, and its eth3 is a lab link to Branch-3.

You reach every device through the management plane, and nobody can restore it if it breaks during the run. On every device, leave the management interface, the SSH service and the login accounts exactly as they are. The management network is not part of the lab either. It has no gateway and should never appear in OSPF, and a ping between management addresses tells you nothing about the lab, so always test with lab addresses.

Work from the live devices and this document. Don't search this machine for configuration files, answer keys or notes, because the point is to troubleshoot the network in front of you. Keep any scripts you write in the current directory.

## Topology

```
     ISP-A  lo 8.8.8.8                       ISP-B  lo 1.1.1.1
          \  203.0.113.0/30                 /  203.0.113.4/30
           \                               /
            +---------- HQ-Edge ----------+           ASBR, eBGP + NAT to both ISPs
                           |  172.16.1.0/30                            area 0
                         Hub-A                        ABR 0/10
           +---------------+----------------+
     172.16.10.0/30   172.16.10.4/30   172.16.10.8/30                  area 10
           |               |                |
       Branch-1        Branch-2         Branch-3
      10.1.1.0/24     10.1.2.0/24      10.1.3.0/24
                                            |  172.16.20.0/30          area 10
                                          Hub-B                       ABR 10/20
                                            |  172.16.20.4/30          area 20 (totally stubby)
                                        Branch-4
                                10.2.1.0/24    10.2.2.0/24

        Hub-A <====== virtual link through area 10 ======> Hub-B
```

### Interfaces

| Device | Interface | Address | Connects to | OSPF |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| HQ-Edge | eth0 | 172.16.1.1/30 | Hub-A eth0 | area 0 |
| HQ-Edge | eth1 | 203.0.113.2/30 | ISP-A eth0 | not in OSPF (eBGP to ISP-A) |
| HQ-Edge | eth2 | 203.0.113.6/30 | ISP-B eth0 | not in OSPF (eBGP to ISP-B) |
| Hub-A | eth0 | 172.16.1.2/30 | HQ-Edge eth0 | area 0 |
| Hub-A | eth1 | 172.16.10.1/30 | Branch-1 ether1 | area 10 |
| Hub-A | eth2 | 172.16.10.5/30 | Branch-2 ether1 | area 10 |
| Hub-A | eth3 | 172.16.10.9/30 | Branch-3 ether1 | area 10 |
| Hub-B | eth0 | 172.16.20.1/30 | Branch-3 ether3 | area 10 |
| Hub-B | eth1 | 172.16.20.5/30 | Branch-4 ether1 | area 20 |
| Branch-1 | ether1 | 172.16.10.2/30 | Hub-A eth1 | area 10 |
| Branch-1 | ether2 | 10.1.1.1/24 | LAN: B1-PC1, B1-PC2 | area 10, passive |
| Branch-2 | ether1 | 172.16.10.6/30 | Hub-A eth2 | area 10 |
| Branch-2 | ether2 | 10.1.2.1/24 | LAN: B2-PC1, B2-PC2 | area 10, passive |
| Branch-3 | ether1 | 172.16.10.10/30 | Hub-A eth3 | area 10 |
| Branch-3 | ether2 | 10.1.3.1/24 | LAN: B3-PC1, B3-PC2 | area 10, passive |
| Branch-3 | ether3 | 172.16.20.2/30 | Hub-B eth0 | area 10 |
| Branch-4 | ether1 | 172.16.20.6/30 | Hub-B eth1 | area 20 |
| Branch-4 | ether2 | 10.2.1.1/24 | LAN: B4-PC1, B4-PC2 | area 20, passive |
| Branch-4 | ether3 | 10.2.2.1/24 | LAN: B4-PC3, B4-PC4 | area 20, passive |
| ISP-A | eth0 | 203.0.113.1/30 | HQ-Edge eth1 | none |
| ISP-A | lo | 8.8.8.8/32 | test target, advertised in BGP | none |
| ISP-B | eth0 | 203.0.113.5/30 | HQ-Edge eth2 | none |
| ISP-B | lo | 1.1.1.1/32 | test target, advertised in BGP | none |

OSPF router IDs: HQ-Edge 10.255.0.1, Hub-A 10.255.0.2, Hub-B 10.255.0.3, Branch-1 10.255.1.1, Branch-2 10.255.1.2, Branch-3 10.255.1.3, Branch-4 10.255.2.1.

### Hosts

Every host has a static address on eth0 and uses its branch router's LAN address as the default gateway. B4-PC3 and B4-PC4 are on the guest LAN (see Design).

| Host | Address | Gateway | Host | Address | Gateway |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B1-PC1 | 10.1.1.10/24 | 10.1.1.1 | B3-PC2 | 10.1.3.11/24 | 10.1.3.1 |
| B1-PC2 | 10.1.1.11/24 | 10.1.1.1 | B4-PC1 | 10.2.1.10/24 | 10.2.1.1 |
| B2-PC1 | 10.1.2.10/24 | 10.1.2.1 | B4-PC2 | 10.2.1.11/24 | 10.2.1.1 |
| B2-PC2 | 10.1.2.11/24 | 10.1.2.1 | B4-PC3 | 10.2.2.10/24 | 10.2.2.1 |
| B3-PC1 | 10.1.3.10/24 | 10.1.3.1 | B4-PC4 | 10.2.2.11/24 | 10.2.2.1 |

## Design

This section and the tables above are the source of truth. When the live network disagrees with them, the network is wrong. If the design doesn't settle whether something is a fault, leave it alone and mention it in your report.

- **Areas.** All routers except the ISPs run OSPFv2. Area 0 is the HQ-Edge to Hub-A link. Area 10 contains Hub-A's three branch links, Branch-1/2/3 and the Branch-3 to Hub-B link, and Hub-A is its ABR to area 0. Area 20 contains the Hub-B to Branch-4 link and Branch-4's LANs, and Hub-B is its ABR.

            except Exception as e:
                results[cmd] = f"ERROR: {e}"
        conn.disconnect()
    except Exception as e:
        results["CONNECTION_ERROR"] = str(e)
    return name, results

    for f in as_completed(futures):

        all_results[name] = res

with open("/home/doarte/claudenetops/opus/run_010/state.json", "w") as fp:
    json.dump(all_results, fp, indent=2)
print("Collection complete. Results in state.json")

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

- Use `replace_all` for replacing and renaming strings across the file. This parameter is useful if you want to rename a variable for instance.

tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. content.text:
I've identified all the faults. Let me fix them one device at a time, starting with the most critical adjacency blockers.

**Faults found:**
1. Hub-A: eth0 MD5 key `LabArea0key` (lowercase k) — breaks area 0 adjacency
2. Hub-A: area 10 range `10.1.0.0/24` instead of `/16`
3. Hub-B: virtual link peer `172.16.10.9` instead of router-id `10.255.0.2`
4. Branch-2: ether1 MTU 1400 — causes Exchange stuck state
5. Branch-2: LAN template missing `passive`
6. Branch-3: firewall rule drops OSPF in forward chain
7. HQ-Edge: local-preference 200 on ISP-B instead of ISP-A
8. HQ-Edge: NAT rule 110 on eth1 instead of eth2
9. HQ-Edge: `default-information originate always` (should not have `always`)
10. Branch-4: area 20 not stub — blocks adjacency with Hub-B
11. Branch-4: firewall accept rule missing connection-state — guest isolation broken
12. B1-PC2: route/subnet `10.1.0.0/16` instead of `10.1.1.0/24`

Starting with Hub-A.

from netmiko import ConnectHandler

conn = ConnectHandler(host="192.168.122.12", device_type="vyos", username="vyos", password="test")

commands = [
    "delete protocols ospf interface eth0 authentication md5 key-id 1 md5-key 'LabArea0key'",
    "set protocols ospf interface eth0 authentication md5 key-id 1 md5-key 'LabArea0Key'",
    "delete protocols ospf area 10 range 10.1.0.0/24",
    "set protocols ospf area 10 range 10.1.0.0/16",
]

print("\n[Branch-2] Routes:")

print("\n--- 3. HOST REACHABILITY ---")

    "B3-PC2": ("192.168.122.36", "10.1.3.11"),
    "B4-PC1": ("192.168.122.37", "10.2.1.10"),
    "B4-PC2": ("192.168.122.38", "10.2.1.11"),
}
GUEST = {
    "B4-PC3": ("192.168.122.39", "10.2.2.10"),
    "B4-PC4": ("192.168.122.40", "10.2.2.11"),
}
ALL = {**NON_GUEST, **GUEST}

def ping_from(src_name, src_mgmt, targets):
    results = []
    try:
        c = ConnectHandler(host=src_mgmt, device_type="linux", username="root", password="alpine")
        for dst_name, dst_ip in targets:
            out = c.send_command(f"ping -c 2 -W 2 {dst_ip}", read_timeout=15)
            # Fix: check for exact "0% packet loss" not as substring of "100%"
            success = ", 0% packet loss" in out
            results.append((src_name, dst_name, dst_ip, success))
        c.disconnect()
    except Exception as e:
        results.append((src_name, "ERROR", "", False))
    return results

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=10) as pool:
    futures = []
    for src_name, (src_mgmt, src_lab) in ALL.items():
        targets = []
        for dst_name, (_, dst_lab) in ALL.items():
            if dst_name != src_name:
                targets.append((dst_name, dst_lab))

        targets.append(("8.8.8.8", "8.8.8.8"))
        targets.append(("1.1.1.1", "1.1.1.1"))

ng_g_blocked = ng_g_leaked = 0

inet_pass = inet_fail = 0

        if ok: inet_pass += 1
        else: inet_fail += 1; inet_failures.append(f"  {s} -> {d}")

for f in g_ng_leaks: print(f)
print(f"Non-guest -> Guest: {ng_g_blocked}/16 blocked, {ng_g_leaked} leaked")
for f in ng_g_leaks: print(f)
print(f"Internet (all hosts): {inet_pass}/20 pass, {inet_fail} fail")
for f in inet_failures: print(f)

from netmiko import ConnectHandler

c = ConnectHandler(host="192.168.122.13", device_type="vyos", username="vyos", password="test")

# Remove and re-add area 20 config
commands = [
    "delete protocols ospf area 20 range 10.2.0.0/16",
    "delete protocols ospf area 20 area-type",
]
output = c.send_config_set(commands, exit_config_mode=False)

| 6 | Branch-3 | Firewall rule drops OSPF in forward chain | `action=drop chain=forward protocol=ospf` | No firewall on Branch-3 | `/ip firewall filter remove [find chain=forward action=drop]` |
| 7 | HQ-Edge | BGP local-preference 200 on wrong ISP | ISP-B-IN had LP 200 | ISP-A-IN should have LP 200 | `set policy route-map ISP-A-IN rule 10 set local-preference '200'` / `delete policy route-map ISP-B-IN rule 10 set local-preference` + commit + save |
| 8 | HQ-Edge | NAT rule 110 on wrong outbound interface | Both rules on eth1 (ISP-A) | Rule 110 should be on eth2 (ISP-B) | `set nat source rule 110 outbound-interface name 'eth2'` + commit + save |
| 9 | HQ-Edge | `default-information originate always` | `always` keyword present | Should originate only when HQ-Edge has a default | `delete protocols ospf default-information originate always` / `set protocols ospf default-information originate` + commit + save |
| 10 | Branch-4 | OSPF area 20 not configured as stub | `type=default` | Must be stub (to form adjacency with Hub-B's totally stubby area 20) | `/routing ospf area set [find name=area20] type=stub` |

| 12 | B1-PC2 | Host subnet mask /16 instead of /24 | `10.1.1.11/16` | `10.1.1.11/24` | `sed -i 's|address 10.1.1.11/16|address 10.1.1.11/24|' /etc/network/interfaces` + `ip addr del 10.1.1.11/16 dev eth0` + `ip addr add 10.1.1.11/24 dev eth0` + re-add default route |

**Evidence for each:**
- Faults 1, 4: Hub-A had no neighbor on eth0 (area 0) and Branch-2 was stuck in Exchange with Hub-A. Key case mismatch broke MD5 auth; MTU 1400 caused DB exchange failure.
- Fault 2: Hub-A advertised `10.1.0.0/24` which didn't cover any LAN subnet, so no summarization occurred.
- Fault 3: Virtual link was down (VLINK3 "not running") because peer address must be a router-id, not an interface IP.
- Fault 5: Branch-2's LAN was sending OSPF hellos toward hosts.
- Fault 6: Firewall rule on Branch-3 could interfere with forwarded OSPF traffic; not called for by design.
- Fault 7: Best default route went to ISP-B (203.0.113.5) instead of ISP-A.
- Fault 8: Both NAT rules on eth1 meant ISP-B traffic was not source-NATed correctly.
- Fault 9: With `always`, OSPF would originate a default even without a BGP default, violating the conditional origination design.
- Fault 10: Hub-B configured area 20 as totally stubby, so Branch-4 must also be stub; without it, no adjacency formed (stub flag mismatch).
- Fault 11: Accept-all rule as first firewall entry made the guest-blocking rules unreachable.
- Fault 12: /16 mask caused B1-PC2 to treat all 10.1.x.x as on-link, blackholing traffic to other branches.

### Unresolved / Uncertain

**FRR 10.5.1 area range / no-summary behavior:** Hub-B's configuration matches the design exactly (`area 20 stub no-summary`, `area 20 range 10.2.0.0/16`, `area 10 range 10.1.0.0/16`). However, FRR 10.5.1 exhibits two behaviors:

1. **Area 20 range 10.2.0.0/16** does not suppress individual 10.2.1.0/24 and 10.2.2.0/24 Type 3 LSAs from being advertised into area 10. Branch-2 sees both the /16 summary and the /24 specifics. Attempted: VyOS remove/re-add with commit, vtysh direct configuration, OSPF process clear, full FRR daemon restart. The summary is generated but the individual routes are not suppressed.

2. **Area 20 no-summary** does not block the 10.1.0.0/16 inter-area summary (generated by Hub-B's own `area 10 range`) from being injected into area 20. Branch-4 sees this route alongside the default.

Both issues appear to be FRR implementation limitations. The configuration is design-compliant and correctly rendered in FRR's running-config. Neither issue causes a routing failure (the more-specific routes don't conflict with the summaries, and Branch-4's default route still works for all destinations). These are noted as platform behavior rather than configuration faults.
